reader.title: Lynching of the gambler Jim in a Colorado mining town
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The narrative describes fifteen or twenty men taking an accused gambler from a guarded lockup and hanging him from a beam over a sidewalk (A1, A4).

As told, a 'committee' of fifteen or twenty men broke into the lockup, took the prisoner accused of shooting an officer, and hanged him until dead, with no legal process, the leader saying he had to 'swing for it' (A1, A4). The account is one recollection reprinted without place, date or race, so the event itself rests on a single source.
Every printing is the same first-person story by one narrator, Ramsey, first given to a Pittsburgh paper and then reprinted (A1, A2, A4, A5); no independent or local report was found.

summary.text: The lynching of the gambler Jim was the hanging of a prisoner by a self-described "committee" in an unnamed Colorado mining town, some months before late November 1880.

According to the only account, fifteen or twenty men took him from a guarded lockup while a coroner's jury sat over the police officer he was accused of shooting, and hanged him from a beam over a sidewalk.
The story is known from a single recollection by a Pittsburgh oil inspector named Ramsey, which ran in several papers as a sketch of Western life.
Ramsey, an oil inspector from Pittsburgh, told a Pittsburgh Dispatch reporter that he had attended a lynching "in a Colorado town" during a visit to the Far West several months earlier.

In his telling, two men quarreled over cards in the gambling saloon of Jim Beggs one evening, and when a police officer told them to quiet down, one of the gamblers drew a revolver and shot him through the heart.
The accused was locked in the "cooler," a frame station-house, under six guards.

Woken early the next morning with the words "wake up or you will miss the lynching," Ramsey found a crowd of miners at the saloon, where a coroner's jury had been impaneled over the officer's body, a coiled rope with a noose lying on top of it.
During the first witness's testimony, a large man in a red flannel shirt picked up the rope and said "Boys, that's enough, come on," and fifteen or twenty men followed him out.
At the lockup the guards said they did not have the keys and let themselves be searched, so the men broke down the door with an axe from a woodpile.
The leader brought the prisoner out with the noose around his neck and the crowd led him down the street to an old building with a beam over the sidewalk.
Asked if he had anything to say, the gambler, addressed as "Jim," offered the $1,000 in his pockets if they would shoot rather than hang him; the leader refused, saying he had "murdered a good man."
When he was first pulled up he grasped the rope, so the men let him down, tied his hands behind him and hanged him again, leaving him for nearly an hour.
Once he was dead, the "committee" sent for a photographer and posed in front of the hanging body, every face recognizable.
His companion was given six hours to leave town.
The coverage shows no arrest of the lynchers and no inquest into the gambler's death.

The earliest printing found, in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer on December 1, 1880, credited the Pittsburgh Dispatch and ran under the headline "Initiation of a Pittsburgh Gentleman into Western Mining Life."
The Point Pleasant Weekly Register reprinted it in January 1881 as "A Colorado Lynching."

Later versions in the Red Cloud Chief of Nebraska in January 1881 and the Somerset Press of Ohio in June 1881 dropped the introduction, credited the Pittsburgh Post and carried the title "An Episode of Border Life," set among humor items.
None of the printings names the town, the date, the dead officer or the race of anyone involved.

The narrative praises the officer, calls the prisoner "the murderer," stresses that the hanging was quiet and orderly, and closes only with the narrator calling it his "first initiation into Western life."

accounts.gist: A Pittsburgh oil inspector recalled being woken to see a lynching in a Colorado town, where a committee took a gambler from the lockup and hanged him for killing a police officer.

accounts.label: Reprinted sketch ('An Episode of Border Life')
accounts.gist: The same first-person story without the introduction naming Ramsey's office or Colorado, credited to the Pittsburgh Post.

framing.detail: The Wheeling paper ran it under 'Initiation of a Pittsburgh Gentleman into Western Mining Life', as 'an interesting story' told to a reporter, with no comment on the lynching.

The narrative praises the dead officer as 'a thoroughly good officer', calls the prisoner 'the murderer' and 'the poor devil', and ends with the narrator hoping it was his last such initiation, without condemning the mob.
Nebraska and Ohio weeklies printed it as filler, 'An Episode of Border Life', beside humor items.

conflicts.note: The earliest printing credits the Dispatch and gives the narrator's occupation; the later reprints credit the Post. The Dispatch version, being earlier and fuller, is likely closer to the original.
The later reprints drop the place; none names the town.

A richly dressed gambler addressed by the leader as 'Jim'; no surname or race given
